sentences.text: Incisivosaurus was a small theropod dinosaur from the early Cretaceous Period of what is now China.
The genus name refers to the animal's prominent, rodent-like front teeth that show wear patterns typical of plant-eaters.
Two juvenile feathered specimens attributed to Incisivosaurus showed long symmetrical vaned feathers on the hands and tails, with the rest of the body covered in downy feathers.
The first Incisivosaurus specimen, a skull named IVPP V13326, was described by Xu et al. in 2002 from the Barremian stage of the Yixian Formation in western Liaoning Province, China.
A 2004 study described Incisivosaurus as having a long snout comprising about half the skull length, a slender lower jaw with a long opening, and distinctive large, flattened front teeth.
In an unweighted cladogram, Incisivosaurus was identified as the sister taxon to Protarchaeopteryx, together forming the most primitive oviraptorosaurians.

Feather development specialist Richard Prum disputed the interpretation that the ribbon-like feather structures on the hands and tails of juvenile Incisivosaurus specimens changed with age, suggesting instead that these structures represented feathers in the process of moulting.

Xu et al. (2010) rebutted the moulting hypothesis, arguing the evidence was problematic due to the absence of previous-generation feathers on the juvenile specimens and that the ribbon-like structures were too large to be pin feathers.
